Ghrita is clarified butter (ghee), an animal-derived (dairy) substance and a base/anupana for medicated ghees. Not a plant; no binomial applicable.
Godanti (literally 'cow's tooth') is the mineral gypsum, hydrated calcium sulphate (CaSO4.2H2O); Godanti Bhasma is its calcined preparation. Mineral, no binomial.
Godugdha is cow's milk (go = cow, dugdha = milk), an animal-derived substance classified in Ksheera varga. No binomial.

Gomeda is a gemstone (hessonite garnet / cinnamon stone, a calcium-aluminium silicate; some sources treat it as zircon); Gomeda Bhasma is its calcined ash, one of the ratna bhasmas. Mineral, no binomial.
Gomutra is cow urine, an animal-derived substance used in Mutra varga and as a shodhana/bhavana medium. No binomial.

Web search of Ayurvedic and general references confirms Gorochana (Gopitta) is a bezoar/gallstone concretion from the gall bladder or bile duct of cattle, equivalent to Calculus bovis. Animal-derived; no binomial.

Ksheerapaka is a preparation method: the drug boiled and reduced in milk. Lasuna Ksheerapaka is garlic (Allium sativum) processed in cow's milk, i.e. a milk-based formulation, not a single botanical drug, so no binomial is assigned.

Page title is the English common name only, with no Sanskrit/Hindi anchor supplied. In Ayurveda licorice is Yashtimadhu = Glycyrrhiza glabra L. An asava (fermented liquid preparation). Although named for Lodhra (Symplocos racemosa), the formulation is a multi-ingredient fermented product with jaggery/dhataki and several other drugs, so no single binomial applies.
Bhasma of loha = incinerated iron, a metallic/mineral calx (largely iron oxide) prepared by shodhana and marana. Not a plant.

A classical fermented asava combining loha bhasma (iron) with numerous plant drugs (Triphala, Trikatu, Musta, Vidanga etc.), jaggery and honey. A herbomineral polyherbal formulation, not a single substance.

Madayantika/Madayanti is the classical name for henna, botanically Lawsonia inermis L. (Lythraceae) in the dominant Dravyaguna reading and in published reviews (JAIMS, 'Comprehensive review on Madayantika (Lawsonia inermis L.)'). Lawsonia inermis L. is POWO-accepted. Flagged contested because some Nighantu commentators equate Madayanti/Madayantika with Mallika, Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton.
A classical herbomineral formulation built on Mandura bhasma (processed iron rust/oxide) with honey and accompanying plant drugs. Mineral-based multi-ingredient preparation, not a plant.
Madhu is honey, an animal (bee) product used as a dravya and anupana across Ayurvedic texts. Classical sources describe eight varieties by bee species; it is not a plant drug and takes no binomial.

A rasaushadhi: a herbomineral 'rasa' formulation containing multiple bhasmas (swarna, abhraka, and others) together with many plant drugs. Multi-ingredient preparation, no single binomial.

Jati/Chameli is standardly Jasminum grandiflorum L. in Ayurvedic dravyaguna (leaf for mouth ulcers, flower, oil), matching this page's leaf-powder/flower-decoction/essential-oil dosage forms; POWO lists Jasminum grandiflorum L. as accepted (some treatments sink it under J. officinale, a taxonomic-rank question rather than a drug-identity dispute). Distinct from Jatiphala (nutmeg).

The one caveat found is that Myristica malabarica (Rampatri, Bombay mace) is used as an adulterant or cheap substitute for Jatiphala in South India; the literature consistently frames this as adulteration, not as a second accepted identity, so it does not make the drug contested. records.identifyBasis: Jatiphala is the dried kernel (nutmeg) of Myristica fragrans Houtt., stated in the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India and standard dravyaguna sources; POWO accepts Myristica fragrans Houtt.

Hindi kachnar / Sanskrit Kanchanara is monographed as Bauhinia variegata L. (stem bark) in the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia and Ayurvedic Formulary of India, following Bhavaprakasha. Classical texts disagree: Dhanvantari Nighantu gives B. purpurea, Raja Nighantu B. acuminata, and Bhavaprakasha describes B. purpurea and B. tomentosa as further varieties, so the trade drug is not species-pure.

Kaharuba (Trinakantamani) is amber, a fossil resin, processed as a pishti by trituration; the page's own cited paper (PMID 35813362) characterises Trinakantamani/Amber Pishti, and the mechanism text cites succinic acid, the amber marker. It is a processed fossil exudate whose extinct source conifers cannot be reduced to one living species, and a pishti is a preparation, not a plant drug.

(= Peristrophe paniculata, Acanthaceae), Abrus precatorius L., and Cardiospermum halicacabum L. Kamsya is bronze, a copper-tin alloy; Kamsya Bhasma is its calcined preparation, filed on the site under Mineral-Metal-Preparations/Bhasmas and described in its own text as copper oxide, tin oxide and mixed Cu-Sn phases. Metallic preparation, no botanical source.

Sanskrit lexica (Monier-Williams via wisdomlib) give Kankataka as armour, an elephant goad, or a mountain name, with no plant identification. Nearby but distinct names exist (Kantakari = Solanum virginianum, Kantaka = Tribulus terrestris, Kankatika = Abutilon sp.), so any match would be a guess at a misspelling. Name-based classification per the task rules: a parpati preparation built on ksharas (alkalis such as yavakshara/sarjikshara) with parada-gandhaka kajjali, cast as a thin flake. Alkali-and-mineral compound formulation, not a plant.
Ksheera (dugdha) is milk, an animal-derived dravya in Ayurvedic materia medica (cow, goat, buffalo milk varieties). Not a botanical drug; no binomial applies.

Kshirabala Taila is a medicated oil of Bala (Sida cordifolia) root decoction, cow's milk and sesame (Sesamum indicum) oil; '101 avarti' denotes 101 rounds of the taila paka. A multi-ingredient oil preparation, not a single plant.
Kukkutanda twak = hen's egg shell; the bhasma is its calcined form (chiefly calcium carbonate). Animal-derived incinerated preparation, not a plant.

Web search shows two well-attested and different identifications: ayushvedah.com and wisdomlib give Kumbhika = Pistia stratiotes (Jalakumbhi, water lettuce), while other dravyaguna sources use Kumbhi/Kumbhika = Careya arborea (Lecythidaceae). Sources genuinely disagree, so no binomial assigned.

Kumud is a Nymphaea (water lily), but sources map it to different species: Nymphaea nouchali (syn. N. stellata) in several reviews, Nymphaea pubescens for the white-flowered kind, and Nymphaea alba in other Ayurvedic monographs; classical usage also blurs Kumuda with Utpala/Indivara. Genus is certain, species is not, so no binomial assigned.

Same drug name as the 'kumud' page. Water lily (Nymphaea sp.), but reputable sources split between Nymphaea nouchali (syn. N. stellata), Nymphaea pubescens and Nymphaea alba, and the name overlaps with Utpala in classical texts. No single species can be asserted.

Web search (wisdomlib entries for Kurabaka/Kuruvaka/Kuravaka, Ayurvedic sources on Sahachara/Jhinti): most commonly read as the red-flowered Barleria cristata, but classical lexicons also gloss Kurabaka as red amaranth (Amaranthus sp.) and some sources give Barleria prionitis; Kuranta nearby is mapped to Celosia argentea. Disagreement is real, so no binomial assigned.

Web search: Ayurvedic college dravyaguna pages, EasyAyurveda and published work on 'sacrificial medicinal grasses' consistently give Kusha/Darbha = Desmostachya bipinnata (Poaceae), one of the Trinapanchamula. Poa cynosuroides is a synonym of the same accepted name, not a rival species.

Web search of classical composition (Rasendra Sara Sangraha, amlapitta chapter): shuddha swarna gairika (purified red ochre) with shunthi (Zingiber officinale), triturated in Nagavalli/betel leaf juice; some market versions add parada, gandhaka, tankana. A herbomineral compound preparation, not a single plant.

Menthol is an isolated chemical constituent (a cyclic monoterpene alcohol), not a botanical drug. It is obtained mainly from Mentha arvensis/M. x piperita oil or made synthetically, so no single plant binomial can be attached to the substance itself as a factual identity claim.

"Morning glory" is a common name for the whole genus Ipomoea (and several related Convolvulaceae genera), hundreds of species. Ayurvedic literature attaches it variously to Ipomoea nil (Krishnabija/Kaladana), Ipomoea mauritiana (Vidari/Bhumikushmanda), Ipomoea sepiaria (Lakshmana) and others. The page carries no Sanskrit or Hindi name to disambiguate, so no binomial can be assigned safely.
Mrigashringa = deer antler/horn; the bhasma is its calcined (incinerated) form, a calcium-rich animal-derived rasaushadhi. Not a plant.

Mukta = pearl; pishti is a levigated (rose-water triturated) preparation. Classed with the ratna/sudha-varga calcium preparations of rasashastra. The raw material is nacre from pearl oysters (Pinctada spp.), i.e. animal in origin but handled as a mineral-type preparation; either way it is not a plant and takes no botanical binomial.

A classical herbo-mineral rasayoga containing the nava-ratna (nine gems: pearl, ruby, coral, emerald, topaz, diamond, sapphire, zircon, cat's-eye) as bhasmas along with metals and multiple plant juices. A multi-ingredient formulation, not a single dravya.
Navayasa Loha (Navayasa Churna/Lauha) is an iron-based compound formulation: loha bhasma with trikatu, triphala, musta and vidanga. Multi-ingredient plus a metal, so no single binomial.

Confirmed. POWO accepts Bacopa monnieri (L.) Wettst. and lists 'water hyssop' and 'Brahmi' among its common names, with Herpestis monniera as a synonym. The Brahmi-versus-Centella asiatica dispute does not reach this page, because the slug is the English name, which attaches only to Bacopa (Centella's English names are gotu kola/Indian pennywort).
